findings.claim: For this unit, you need to know three methods — job, flow and lean production — plus the idea of just in time (JIT) as a way of making production more efficient.
findings.truth: The spec lists two methods of production: job and flow. Lean production and JIT sit under 'Efficiency in production'. A student who answers 'lean' to a question on methods of production would not be credited. The lesson itself says later that lean 'is not a separate method so much as a mindset'.

findings.claim: For a 6-mark Analyse question you can now pull on more than one factor, but markers still reward a developed chain of reasoning
findings.truth: 'You can now' implies a change of assessment rule that the spec does not make, and 'markers still reward' is an invented examiner claim. The same fabricated 'new approach' pattern was found in the sibling unit business-real-world.
findings.evidence: spec 2.2 assessment section; no such statement anywhere in the spec

findings.claim: [5].marks ends 'Around four minutes of the answer should be spent on the evaluative judgement itself.'
findings.truth: Invented timing advice, appended to the bottom band of the ladder where it does not belong. Paper 1 gives 1 hour 45 minutes for 90 marks, so a 9-mark answer is worth about 10 minutes in total. AQA publishes no per-part timing.

findings.claim: Examiners advise around four minutes on the evaluative judgement itself; a one-line conclusion is not enough.
findings.truth: A fabricated examiner claim. AQA gives no per-part timing guidance in the specification.

findings.claim: [5].marks ends 'Around four minutes of the answer should focus on the evaluative judgement.'
findings.truth: The same invented timing advice as F3, appended to the bottom band of the ladder.

findings.claim: John Lewis built its ‘Never Knowingly Undersold’ reputation on exactly this principle — every partner (employee) sees quality as part of their role.
findings.truth: 'Never Knowingly Undersold' was a price-matching pledge, introduced in 1925 and used until August 2022, with a refined version returning in 2024. It was about price, not quality, so it is the wrong example for TQM.

findings.claim: Toyota’s Prius recalls in 2009–2010, covering around 8 million cars worldwide, cost the company an estimated $2 billion
findings.truth: The 2009-11 Toyota recalls covered about 9 million vehicles across many models (Camry, Corolla, RAV4, Highlander, Tundra and others, plus Lexus). The Prius recall on its own was an anti-lock brake software fix on about 133,000 cars in the US and 52,000 in Europe. Toyota did say losses could reach US$2 billion, but for the whole programme, not the Prius.

findings.claim: [12] 'What did Toyota's 2009-10 Prius recall cost the company?' / 'About $2 billion across approximately 8 million vehicles worldwide.'
findings.truth: The same error as F7 in the flashcard: the figures belong to the whole recall programme (about 9 million vehicles), not the Prius brake recall.

findings.claim: [9].a 'Millions of cars were recalled, fines exceeded $30bn, and trust took years to rebuild.'
findings.truth: $33.3 billion (as at 1 June 2020) is the total of fines, penalties, financial settlements and buyback costs. The US criminal fine alone was $2.8 billion. About 11 million vehicles carried the defeat device.

findings.claim: [4] 'Analyse the impact on a growing UK franchise such as Greggs of introducing Total Quality Management across all stores.'
findings.truth: Greggs is mainly a company-managed chain. It does run a minority franchised estate (travel hubs, Primark and supermarket sites), so the label is not false, but it is a weak example of a franchise next to McDonald's, which the lesson already uses correctly.

findings.claim: [5].marks ends 'Around four minutes of the answer should focus on the evaluative judgement.'
findings.truth: The same invented timing advice as F3 and F5.

findings.claim: a single bad review can outweigh five good ones
findings.truth: An invented ratio with no source. The lesson's own flashcard says 'several good ones', which is the defensible form.
findings.evidence: no source found; internal inconsistency with flashcard [11]

findings.claim: Tesco’s ‘out-of-stock tweet’ replies during the 2021 supply squeeze are a textbook example of both the risks and the skill needed to handle social service well.
findings.truth: No such named Tesco episode can be found. The 2021 UK supply-chain shortages and empty shelves are well documented, so the teaching point stands once the invented case study is removed.
findings.evidence: no source found for the named incident

findings.claim: The Guide Dogs charity used a similar engagement philosophy when designing their shops, training volunteers to have the longer conversations supporters expect from a charity.
findings.truth: This claim about a named charity cannot be verified from any public source, and it sits in the same family as F13. Two options: delete the sentence, because the John Lewis example in the same paragraph already carries the point, or keep it as a soft illustration. Recommendation: delete it.
findings.ruling: Unverifiable named-charity claim deleted; the John Lewis example carries the point.

findings.claim: This is also the sales process in practice: attention, interest, desire, action.
findings.truth: AIDA is a promotion model. The spec's sales-process content is product knowledge, customer engagement and post-sales services. AIDA is not wrong as a description of how a customer moves to a purchase, so no edit, but the lesson should not lead with it.

findings.claim: You will not be asked to draw or interpret a stock control chart in the exam, but you should be able to evaluate the use of JIT for a given business.
findings.truth: Correct, and worth recording because the retro brief expected bar gate stock graphs. This spec explicitly excludes them, so this unit has no stock-graph figures to recompute.
findings.evidence: spec 3.3.2 line 901: 'Students will not be asked to draw or interpret stock control charts.'

summary: All 20 knowledge-check keys, all four match sets and every calculation are correct (0.40 + 0.40 = 0.80 per loaf; 5% of 28,000 = 1,400; 120/5,000 = 2.4%; 14,400/20,000 = 72%), and every practice tariff (1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 12) is a real AQA tariff with no paper or SPaG claim. The damage is four invented 'four minutes' timing claims planted in mark schemes and an exam tip, a fabricated 'you can now' rule change, three wrong real-world facts (Toyota's recall attributed to the Prius at 8 million cars, VW's $33bn total costs called fines, Never Knowingly Undersold used as a TQM example), lean production taught as a method of production, and two unverifiable case studies.
